for_davis: Three threads land on your plan today. (1) The safety lens: Anthropic's AI-worm demo is the frontier of your runtime-mechanics exam territory — agents that self-replicate across devices are agentic loops with no off switch. Read it as a design lesson for sprints 3-5, not doom: every agent you build should assume hostile environments. (2) The DC angle: Anthropic drafting its own federal bill — with Commerce Department evaluations and federal preemption of state laws — is exactly the regulatory terrain your future gov-contracting employers will live in. Track the preemption fight; regulated-industry AI is your wedge. (3) The tool verdict: a price-and-plan check updated today confirms your stack is the sensible one — Claude Code for delegated long-horizon work, Cursor for in-editor collaboration — and the $8 Codex entry point is worth knowing about. (4) The model layer keeps getting cheaper: MiniMax's M3.1 Flash (3x faster, 70% cheaper) continues the DeepSeek Flash trend from yesterday — your sprint 3-5 projects will have no shortage of cheap model firepower.
headline: Anthropic demos AI worms — then drafts the law to stop them; MiniMax joins the price war.

stories.summary: Anthropic's offensive research team disclosed that it built a malicious AI program that spread autonomously through internet-connected smart TVs, splitting parts of itself across 15 Android TV boxes and functioning by borrowing a little compute from each. The team says the same could work on other ordinary devices: IoT hardware is patched rarely and patched badly, so AI worms would be harder to kill than phones or laptops. The team believes this level of capability on low-power devices is 'months away' at current trends. Security experts are split on urgency — Joshua Saxe (ex-Meta AI security) warns the cybersecurity community isn't taking it seriously enough.
stories.title: Anthropic's red team splits an 'AI worm' across 15 smart TVs, says the real thing is months away
stories.why_it_matters: This is your agent-runtime exam territory weaponized: self-replicating agents with no off switch, living in devices nobody patches. It's the dark mirror of yesterday's Anthropic agent exploits — and a design lesson. Every agent you build in sprints 3-5 has to assume hostile, permissioned environments, not friendly ones.

stories.summary: Anthropic has been quietly pitching Capitol Hill on draft federal AI safety legislation — its own version of the framework it has promoted since June. Per the draft seen by Politico: the government could ask a federal judge to block a model's release or use, but only on a narrow trigger — foreseeable, imminent risk of $1B+ in damages or death/serious harm to 50+ people, tied to biological weapons, loss of control, or cyberattack. Independent evaluators registered with the Commerce Department would periodically assess frontier models and report imminent risk within 72 hours. Crucially, the draft bars any other federal agency from unilaterally suspending a model's development, deployment or internal use, and would preempt some state safety rules — a reversal for Anthropic, which previously backed state-level legislation. The bill has no sponsors yet and Congress is in recess until after the midterms.
stories.title: Anthropic lobbies Congress on its own federal AI safety bill — narrow kill-switch, Commerce-run evaluations
stories.why_it_matters: The lab is now writing the law that would govern it — a classic regulatory-maneuver move worth watching with DC eyes. The preemption fight (federal rules overriding state ones) and Commerce Department evaluation mandates define the compliance world your future employers will operate in. Regulated industries are where your health-tech background is a differentiator.

stories.summary: MiniMax launched an updated M3.1 Flash on Oct 19, claiming improvements in agentic tasks, programming, cybersecurity, inference speed and usage costs: nearly triple the online inference speed and a 70% reduction in usage costs versus the previous version. It follows yesterday's DeepSeek V4.1-Flash-1017 release — the second cheap-and-fast model aimed squarely at coding agents in two days. (Vendor-claimed benchmarks; treat the numbers as direction, not fact.)
stories.title: MiniMax launches updated M3.1 Flash: 3x faster inference, 70% cheaper, tuned for agentic tasks
stories.why_it_matters: The cheap-model layer your sprint 3-5 projects will run on is getting crowded in a good way: two aggressive fast-and-cheap releases in two days, both aimed at agentic coding. For your builds, this means the model is increasingly a commodity you swap, not a constraint you design around.

stories.summary: A vendor-pricing-verified guide (prices checked Oct 19 on each vendor's own site) frames the choice crisply: Claude Code and OpenAI's Codex are agents built for delegation — long-horizon tasks you hand off — while Cursor is built for collaboration, keeping you in the loop keystroke by keystroke, and many teams run both. Cheapest paid plans: Codex Go at $8/month (with a free tier including GPT-6 Luna), Cursor Plus at $8/month, Claude Pro at $20/month. Codex is the suggested default for beginners; Claude Code for Claude subscribers and long hands-off sessions; Cursor for those who want editor and agent as one product. Companion data point from BenchLM's CursorBench 4.0 leaderboard: on Cursor's own benchmark, Anthropic models take the top four spots, with Claude Fable 5.1 scoring 51.8 versus Cursor's Composer 2.5 at 27.7.
stories.title: Claude Code vs Codex vs Cursor, refreshed Oct 19: delegation vs collaboration, priced to the dollar
stories.why_it_matters: This validates your stack exactly as you're using it: Claude Code for delegation, Cursor for collaboration. Two things to pocket: Codex's $8 entry (with a free tier) is the cheapest way to try a second agent paradigm, and the benchmark gap between Anthropic's models and Cursor's own Composer is why Claude Code stays your primary exam-and-building tool.

tldr: Anthropic dominated the day from both ends: its red team showed an AI worm spreading across 15 smart TVs ('months away' from real), while its lobbyists pitched Congress a draft federal AI safety bill with a narrow $1B/50-lives kill-switch. MiniMax's M3.1 Flash kept the cheap-model race moving (3x faster, 70% cheaper), and an Oct-19 pricing check confirms your Claude Code + Cursor stack is the sensible default.
